anchorPassages.text:
I am that man; I know you near
Ears to the blind, they say, are eyes.
O dread to see and dread to hear!
Oh sirs, I am no outlaw under ban.
Who can he be—Zeus save us!—this old man?
No favourite of fate,
That ye should envy his estate,
O, Sirs, would any happy mortal, say,
Grope by the light of other eyes his way,
Or face the storm upon so frail a stay?
Wast thou then sightless from thy birth?
Evil, methinks, and long
Thy pilgrimage on earth.
Yet add not curse to curse and wrong to wrong.
I warn thee, trespass not
Within this hallowed spot,
Lest thou shouldst find the silent grassy glade
Where offerings are laid,
Bowls of spring water mingled with sweet mead.
Thou must not stay,
Come, come away,
Tired wanderer, dost thou heed?
(We are far off, but sure our voice can reach.)
If aught thou would’st beseech,
Speak where ’tis right; till then refrain from speech.

anchorPassages.note: The name that made him famous now makes him untouchable.
anchorPassages.text:
Know’st one of Laius’—
Ha! Who!
Seed of Labdacus—
Oh Zeus!
The hapless Oedipus.
Art he?
Whate’er I utter, have no fear of me.
Begone!
O wretched me!
Begone!
O daughter, what will hap anon?
Forth from our borders speed ye both!
How keep you then your troth?
Heaven’s justice never smites
Him who ill with ill requites.
But if guile with guile contend,
Bane, not blessing, is the end.
Arise, begone and take thee hence straightway,
Lest on our land a heavier curse thou lay.

anchorPassages.text:
O sirs! ye suffered not my father blind,
Albeit gracious and to ruth inclined,
Knowing the deeds he wrought, not innocent,
But with no ill intent;
Yet heed a maiden’s moan
Who pleads for him alone;
My eyes, not reft of sight,
Plead with you as a daughter’s might
You are our providence,
O make us not go hence!
O with a gracious nod
Grant us the nigh despaired-of boon we crave!
Hear us, O hear,
By all that ye hold dear,
Wife, children, homestead, hearth and God!
Where will you find one, search ye ne’er so well,
Who ’scapes perdition if a god impel!

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Heaven’s justice never smites / Him who ill with ill requites” slowly and put it in my own words: The elders say heaven's justice never strikes a person who pays back a wrong with a wrong. They use that rule to justify driving him out after they promised safety. Next, craft. I notice they answer Oedipus's “How keep you then your troth?” (line 221) not by keeping the promise but by renaming the expulsion as justice. The strongest word is “requites”: “ill with ill requites” turns their broken welcome into a repayment, as if his name were itself a wrong they may lawfully pay back. Then, effect. What do lines 222–223 reveal about the elders' fear? My answer: This is the elders' fear: a name alone condemns him, his story has traveled ahead of him, and they treat expulsion as just requital rather than a broken troth.

items.answerGuidance: What they should now pursue.

items.text: What does Oedipus offer to teach the elders, if they will let him speak?
items.lookFor: The worship due to this place, as he has learned it
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: The worship due to this place, as he has learned it.

items.text: Why does the Chorus break its promise of safety?
items.lookFor: Fear of pollution, once they hear his name, outweighs the promise they made while he was still an unknown wanderer. Before the revelation they had said, “Against thy will no man shall drive thee hence.” After he names Laius, Labdacus, and himself, they cry “Begone!” and defend the reversal with “Heaven’s justice never smites / Him who ill with ill requites.” The name, not a new deed in the grove, is what changes their mind.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Fear of pollution, once they hear his name, outweighs the promise they made while he was still an unknown wanderer. Before the revelation they had said, “Against thy will no man shall drive thee hence.” After he names Laius, Labdacus, and himself, they cry “Begone!” and defend the reversal with “Heaven’s justice never smites / Him who ill with ill requites.” The name, not a new deed in the grove, is what changes their mind.

items.text: Why does Antigone, rather than Oedipus, make the longest plea after the elders turn on him?
items.lookFor: She can still see, she is not the infamous name they fear, and she can appeal to their pity as a daughter. “My eyes, not reft of sight, / Plead with you as a daughter’s might,” she says, and she reminds them that they already knew something of “the deeds he wrought, not innocent, / But with no ill intent.” The speech tries to separate the man in front of them from the story that has gone ahead of him.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: She can still see, she is not the infamous name they fear, and she can appeal to their pity as a daughter. “My eyes, not reft of sight, / Plead with you as a daughter’s might,” she says, and she reminds them that they already knew something of “the deeds he wrought, not innocent, / But with no ill intent.” The speech tries to separate the man in front of them from the story that has gone ahead of him.

items.text: What does “Parodos (lines 115–248)” suggest about the elders' fear? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: An inference that the elders’ fear is religious before it is personal: they dread the goddesses’ anger at a trespass, and once they hear his name, dread of pollution outweighs pity.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Their fear starts as reverence for the goddesses, “The Maids in awe of whom each mortal cowers” (line 124), past whom they move “with averted eye” (line 126). When they hear his name, the same fear turns on him: “Lest on our land a heavier curse thou lay” (line 227). They fear what his presence may bring on the whole land, not what he might do with his hands.

items.text: Find one example of conflict in “Parodos (lines 115–248)”. What does it reveal about the elders' fear that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: A specific clash, such as the elders’ “Begone!” against his “How keep you then your troth?”, explained for what it shows: fear is strong enough to make decent men break their word.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: When the elders cry “Begone!” (line 216), Oedipus answers, “How keep you then your troth?” (line 221). A plain statement would say only that they changed their minds. The exchange shows that they know they promised “Against thy will no man shall drive thee hence” (line 165), and that fear makes them break that promise while still claiming the gods are on their side.

items.text: How does the characterization in “Parodos (lines 115–248)” shape what we understand about the elders' fear?
items.lookFor: How the elders are drawn as pious, nervous and quick to judge (they hunt, shout, then shelter behind “the decrees of Heaven”), so their fear reads as communal panic rather than cruelty.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The elders enter like a search party (“Ha! Where is he? Look around!”, line 115) and call the unseen man “The wretch profane!” (line 132) before they have met him. At the end they admit pity yet hide behind piety: “as we reverence the decrees of Heaven / We cannot say aught other than we said” (lines 247–248). They are not villains; theirs is the fear of a community that believes it must protect itself from the gods.

items.text: In the passage that opens with “Ha!”, why might Sophocles have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Two words from lines 115–133 with their connotations, such as “all-presumptuous” (arrogance toward the gods), “profane” (unclean), “scan” (a hunt) or “hushed” (fearful reverence).
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The word “all-presumptuous” (line 117) accuses the stranger of arrogance toward the gods, not only of wandering into the wrong place. The word “profane” (line 132) goes further and marks him as unclean. Both words judge a man the elders have not yet seen, so the diction shows fear running ahead of knowledge.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Parodos (lines 115–248)”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: The turn is the naming: pressed for his family, Oedipus says he is of Laius and Labdacus, and the elders reverse their promise. The effect is that Antigone must plead and the question of his staying is open again.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The turn is caused by the elders’ demand to know his family: “Say of what stock thou comest, what man’s son” (line 204). When he answers “The hapless Oedipus” (line 213), they cry “Begone!” (line 216). The promise of safety collapses, Antigone pleads, and the elders end by saying they “cannot say aught other than we said” (line 248). His fate is left for someone else to settle.

items.text: How does “Parodos (lines 115–248)” build on “Prologue (lines 1–114)”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A cause-and-effect link: in the Prologue the stranger left to fetch the local men who would decide; the Parodos is that decision, or Oedipus’s withheld name becomes the question forced out here.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: In the Prologue the stranger went to “seek the burghers” (line 78), who “will soon decide / Whether thou art to rest or go thy way” (lines 79–80). The Parodos delivers that decision. The burghers enter searching (“I search and search in vain,” line 133) and, once they know his name, decide he must go. The Prologue’s open question becomes the Parodos’s verdict.

items.text: In “Parodos (lines 115–248)”, what can we infer about a character's motives from what they say on stage about the elders' fear, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: A motive read beneath a claim: the elders claim divine justice, but their next line shows fear for their land; Oedipus delays his name because he knows what it will do.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The elders say they are acting justly, as if expelling him only repaid a wrong: “Heaven’s justice never smites / Him who ill with ill requites” (lines 222–223). The lines that follow show the real motive, fear for their own land (line 227). Oedipus, for his part, holds back his name (“Forbear, nor urge me further to reveal,” line 199) because he knows what hearing it will do to them.

items.text: Go back to the bell-ringer question (Is it fair to judge someone by what we have heard about them?). Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer anchored in a line where the elders judge by rumour, such as the rumour they hunt or the instant “Begone!” after the name, with a sentence on what changed the student’s mind.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: At first I said judging by reputation is unfair but sometimes necessary. The Parodos shows how rumour outruns evidence. The elders hunt a man because “But now some godless man, / ’Tis rumoured, here abides” (lines 128–129), and they expel Oedipus the moment he says his name, before he has done anything in their sight. Antigone’s line “Knowing the deeds he wrought, not innocent, / But with no ill intent” (lines 230–231) changed my mind: judging by the name skips the question of intent.

items.text: Are the elders right to fear Oedipus? Defend your view with evidence from this section.
items.lookFor: A position on whether the fear is justified by what is on stage (a trespass on holy ground, a name they believe polluted) against what is not (no new wrong; the plea about intent), with a counter-line.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: partly. They are right to guard the grove, since he sat “Within this hallowed spot” (line 149), and in their belief the goddesses punish trespass. They are wrong to fear the man himself, who tells them, “Whate’er I utter, have no fear of me” (line 215), and has harmed no one in their sight. Counter-line: in their religion a polluted man could bring “a heavier curse” on the land (line 227) whatever his intent, so their fear makes sense on its own terms.

items.text: Consider this reading of the scene (a claim, not a line from the text): A name alone condemns him: his story travels ahead of him. How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the scene.
items.lookFor: A stand with two lines: the reversal follows the name alone (lines 213–216). A careful qualification notes that what travels ahead of him is a belief about pollution, not only gossip.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: largely agree. The elders promised safety (line 165) and reversed it the moment they heard “The hapless Oedipus” (line 213), crying “Begone!” (line 216). Nothing he did changed; only the name did. A qualification: what goes ahead of him is not just a story but a belief about pollution, which they defend with “Heaven’s justice” (line 222). They think they are obeying the gods, not repeating gossip.

items.text: Which character in “Parodos (lines 115–248)” acts most wisely in the matter of the elders' fear, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: A named standard, such as fairness (judging deeds and intent, not names), applied to two of Oedipus, Antigone and the elders, with a line for each.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: by the standard of fairness, Antigone acts most wisely. She grants that her father’s deeds were “not innocent” (line 230) but insists they were done “with no ill intent” (line 231), asking the elders to judge the man and not the name. By the same standard the elders act least wisely: they break their own word, “Against thy will no man shall drive thee hence” (line 165), as soon as fear outweighs it. A student who chooses piety as the standard could rank the elders higher, since they cite “the decrees of Heaven” (line 247).

items.text: You are directing “Parodos (lines 115–248)”. Make two staging choices (a line delivery, a movement, a light or sound cue) and explain how each shapes the audience's view of the elders' fear.
items.lookFor: Two staging choices tied to lines, such as the chorus scattering to search, a silence before the name, or a collective recoil, each with its effect on how we see the elders’ fear.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: (1) Bring the elders on in scattered clusters, peering into corners on “Every nook and corner scan!” (line 116), so their fear looks like a manhunt before we see the old blind man they are hunting. (2) Hold a long silence after “Know’st one of Laius’—” (line 209), then have the whole chorus step back together on “Ha! Who!” (line 210). The physical recoil lets the audience feel how a name alone pushes people away.

items.text: Write your own questions about “Parodos (lines 115–248)”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions, each answerable from lines 115–248: one recall, one why/how and one should/what-if, different in kind.
followUps: Which of your questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Model set. Recall: What do the elders order once Oedipus names himself? (“Begone!”, line 216.) Why/how: Why does Antigone stress that the deeds were done “with no ill intent” (line 231)? (She separates guilt from the act.) Should/what if: Should the elders have kept the promise of line 165 once they knew his name? (Answers weigh a sworn word against a community’s fear.)

items.text: Connect “Parodos (lines 115–248)”, with its focus on the elders' fear, to law against force: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Sophocles need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment about law against force, the theme the question names. So far the elders use commands and custom, not hands, and no one has tried force; a strong answer says what Sophocles must show next.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: the link is present but weak so far. The elders speak for rule and custom, “Honour whatso’er the State / Honours, all she frowns on hate” (lines 177–178), and use words, not hands, even when they cry “Begone!”. No one has yet tried to take anyone by force, so law has not been tested against force. To strengthen the link, Sophocles would need to show someone choosing force where law or a sworn word should govern, and show how the land answers.

items.text: Is the conflict in “Parodos (lines 115–248)” effective in presenting the elders' fear, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: A judgment of the confrontation against a stated criterion (does it build tension through rhythm and reversal, or is the shouting overdone?), with one line that meets it and one that might miss it.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: effective. The broken half-lines “Know’st one of Laius’— / Ha! Who! / Seed of Labdacus— / Oh Zeus!” (lines 209–212) build tension like a cross-examination, so the reversal feels forced out of the elders rather than announced. Counter-line: the repeated “Begone!” (lines 216 and 218) could feel heavy-handed to a modern reader unless it is played as panic rather than cruelty.

items.text: Compare how “Parodos (lines 115–248)” treats the elders' fear with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Oedipus at Colonus see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A named comparison (a text, film or event where a community judges someone by reputation) and one thing the Parodos sees that the other misses, tied to a line.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: In The Crucible, Salem condemns people largely on rumour and fear. The Parodos sees something that play leaves in the background: the accusers are frightened, and they pity the people they expel. The elders say, “Surely we pity thee and him alike” (line 245), and still send them away. Sophocles shows how decent people can do an unfair thing for what they believe is a sacred reason.

items.text: Predict what “Episode 1 (lines 249–694)” will bring, using two clues from this scene. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction from two clues in this scene, such as the elders’ pity despite their ruling and their order to speak only “where ’tis right,” checked after reading.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Clue 1: the elders admit, “Surely we pity thee and him alike” (line 245), though they will not change their ruling, so Oedipus may try to turn that pity into a reversal. Clue 2: they told him, “If aught thou would’st beseech, / Speak where ’tis right” (lines 157–158), so the next scene will probably be his defence in words. A sharper prediction asks whether someone with more authority than the elders will be asked to decide.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of “Parodos (lines 115–248)” (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about the elders' fear?
items.lookFor: An adaptation that keeps the core situation: a group turns on a newcomer the moment it learns his notorious name, after promising him safety. It names two details that must stay: the broken promise and a family member pleading about intent.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Volunteers at a small-town shelter welcome an old blind man until someone recognises his name from a decades-old scandal; within minutes they tell him to leave “for everyone’s safety.” His daughter stands up and argues that he did terrible things without knowing what he was doing. Two things must stay: the promise of safety given before the name was known (line 165), and the plea that separates the deed from the intent (lines 230–231).

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.
